Celebration · Osceola County

The short version for Celebration

A paver walkway in Celebration runs $14.00–$24.00 per sq ft (Q3 2026 Cost Index); entry steps are rebuilt per riser. The front walk is part of the streetscape the Design Guidelines protect, so material, pattern and border go through the Architectural Review Committee (third Monday). The work is mostly replacing 1996–2006 walks lifted by the street oaks and rebuilding stoops whose risers have settled unevenly.

Walks in the village pattern

Celebration's front walks were laid in a brick-look running bond with a border that varies by village, from the sidewalk to a stoop of two or three risers. Thirty years of oak roots and settled base have lifted panels and opened joints; the repair is a lift-and-relay on a compacted 4-inch base with edge restraint set on the base on both sides, the original units reset, replacements from a matched lot at the ends. Where a root has lifted a section 2 inches or more we install a root barrier and reset over it rather than cut the root (Live Oak Roots and Driveways: What Lifts a Slab and What to Do). Steps: block risers on a footing, paver treads with a nosing, riser heights equalized within ¼ inch, which is usually why the old stoop felt wrong.

Review and permits

The ARC packet for a walk is a sketch on the survey, product, pattern, border and a sample; Town Hall (407-566-1200 ext. 2206) has the village guidelines. A private walk on the lot needs no county permit; a section that crosses the public sidewalk strip is the county's right-of-way under LDC 4.12.2 and is confirmed with the Building Office (407-742-0200). Pages: Celebration (CROA), Unincorporated Osceola County, HOA / ARC Packet Checklist.

Worked example

A West Village walk and stoop

42-foot front walk, 4 feet wide (168 square feet) in tumbled clay-look pavers lifted at one oak, plus a three-riser stoop with a 1½-inch difference between risers. Walk lifted and relaid over a root barrier on a rebuilt base ($9.00–$16.00 per sq ft: $1,510 to $2,690); stoop rebuilt with block risers and paver treads ($250 to $450 per step: $750 to $1,350). Two days after ARC approval. Ranges from the Q3 2026 index.

Can I change my front walk's pattern in Celebration?

With ARC approval, within the village's palette. The Design Guidelines treat the front walk as part of the streetscape, so a change in material, pattern or border is reviewed at the monthly meeting with a sample. A like-for-like repair in the same units is maintenance and moves faster.

Streetscape

Front walks are part of the streetscape here

In most subdivisions a front walk is a private detail. In Celebration it is part of a designed streetscape with a consistent relationship between the sidewalk, the front walk, the porch and the street trees, and the architectural guidance treats it that way. Width, alignment, material and the way the walk meets the public sidewalk all get reviewed, and a walk that is wider or more elaborate than the pattern is the kind of thing that comes back with conditions.

Practically, the work is small and fussy. A typical Celebration front walk is three to four feet wide and fifteen to thirty feet long, with a step or two at the porch, tree roots to route around, and irrigation directly under the route. The cutting is a large share of the labour because of the border course and the transition at the public sidewalk, which has to stay at the existing elevation.

Steps, risers and the details that fail

Paver steps fail in three predictable ways. The riser height varies because the treads were set to the ground rather than to a consistent rise, which is both ugly and a trip hazard. The tread nosing is unsupported and works loose under foot traffic. And water gets behind the riser face and pushes it out over a few wet seasons.

What we do instead: set a consistent rise and run for the whole flight, build the step core in poured concrete or compacted base with a solid bearing under each nosing, bond the riser face rather than relying on sand, and drain behind the risers so water leaves rather than collecting. On a porch with existing concrete steps, capping with large-format treads is often better than rebuilding, and that is the detail shown in the entry-step photograph in the gallery.

On this job

The transition to the public sidewalk

A Celebration front walk meets a public sidewalk that is part of the community's streetscape and sits at a fixed elevation. The private walk has to arrive at that elevation cleanly, with no lip, no change of slope at the joint and no cut into the sidewalk itself. Where the existing walk has settled and the sidewalk has not, the new walk is built back up to meet it rather than the other way round.

That junction is also where a mitred or squared border detail either looks deliberate or looks improvised, so it is set out on the ground with string before any base goes down. It is a small area that gets looked at more than any other part of the job.

Questions we get about this

Who approves a walkway change?

The CROA Architectural Review Committee; Town Hall has the village-specific guidelines.

Can you fix the lifted section without redoing the whole walk?

Yes; a lift-and-relay over a root barrier on the affected run, with matched units at the seam.

Is a permit needed?

Not for a private walk on the lot; the strip across the public sidewalk is county right-of-way and is confirmed first.

How much is a stoop rebuild?

About $250 to $450 per riser plus the landing, in paver treads; travertine or porcelain treads add material.

Can I widen my front walk?

Possibly, with approval. The community's guidance treats the front walk as part of the streetscape, so width and alignment are reviewed rather than assumed.

Can my concrete porch steps be capped with pavers?

Often yes, with large-format treads bonded to sound concrete. It avoids demolition and gives a consistent rise, which a rebuilt flight does not always achieve.
